question: Where can I hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer near me?
body:
## Direct Answer

You can hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer through fractional-executive marketplaces (Chief Outsiders, Go Fractional, Bolster, Continuum, TechCXO), RevOps and GTM consultancies, executive-search firms with interim practices, and warm referrals from investors, peer CEO groups, and your own LinkedIn network. "Near me" matters far less than it used to: most fractional CROs work remotely across a portfolio of clients, so the right question is not who is geographically closest but who has closed deals in your motion, price band, and stage. Start with a marketplace for speed and a vetted bench, or a referral for trust and speed-to-fit, then run a structured 2-to-4 week trial engagement before signing a longer retainer.

A fractional CRO is a part-time senior revenue leader who owns your entire go-to-market engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, pricing, and forecasting — for a fraction of a full-time executive's cost and commitment. Companies reach for one when revenue has outgrown the founder's selling instincts but can't yet justify a $300K-plus base plus equity for a full-time CRO. This essay maps every credible channel to find one, how to vet them, what they cost, and how to structure the engagement so you get a revenue operator and not an expensive advisor who leaves slides behind.

## What exactly is a fractional CRO and when do you actually need one?

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is an experienced revenue executive who works with your company on a part-time, ongoing basis — typically one to three days a week — carrying real accountability for pipeline, conversion, and revenue targets rather than just offering advice. Unlike a consultant who diagnoses and departs, a fractional CRO sits inside your operating rhythm: they run the forecast call, coach the AEs, own the number, and hire their eventual full-time replacement. The "fractional" part refers only to their time allocation, not their seniority or their ownership of outcomes.

You need one when the symptoms are structural, not tactical. The classic triggers are a founder-led sales motion hitting its ceiling (usually somewhere between $1M and $10M ARR), a first sales hire who is missing quota because there's no system around them, a board pushing for predictable forecasting before a raise, or a go-to-market that works but can't be explained — you close deals but nobody can tell you why or repeat it. If your problem is "we need more leads this quarter," you need a demand-gen contractor. If your problem is "our entire revenue engine has no operating system and I keep being the only person who can close," you need a fractional CRO. The distinction determines which of the channels below you should even bother searching. For a deeper breakdown of the role boundaries, see the [RevOps leadership roles guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-leadership-roles).

![Where can I hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer near me — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9313-b1.jpg)


The stage fit is real and worth respecting. A pre-revenue startup rarely needs a CRO of any fraction — it needs founders selling and learning. A company north of ~$15-20M ARR usually needs the full-time version. The fractional sweet spot is the messy middle where the cost of a wrong full-time hire is catastrophic and the cost of staying founder-dependent is a stalled growth curve.

## Where do you actually find fractional CROs? The five channels ranked

There are five reliable channels, and they trade off speed, vetting rigor, cost, and fit in predictable ways. The fastest path is a fractional-executive marketplace; the highest-trust path is a warm referral; the rest sit in between.

![Where can I hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer near me — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9313-b2.jpg)


**Marketplaces and fractional-executive platforms.** These are purpose-built benches of vetted part-time executives. Chief Outsiders is the largest and most established for fractional CMO/CRO-type roles, with a heavy mid-market and PE-backed focus. Bolster (co-founded by former Return Path CEO Matt Blumberg) matches startups with fractional and interim execs and is investor-friendly. Go Fractional, Continuum, and TechCXO round out the category, each with slightly different stage and industry tilts. The advantage is speed and a pre-screened bench; the tradeoff is that marketplaces take a margin and their vetting is for general credibility, not for your specific motion. See the [go-to-market operating model overview](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/gtm-operating-model) for how to brief a marketplace on your motion so their match is precise.

**RevOps and GTM consultancies.** Boutique firms that live in revenue operations often place or embed fractional revenue leaders. This channel is strong when your gap is as much systems and process as it is leadership — the firm brings a bench plus a playbook plus tooling expertise. The tradeoff is that a firm's incentive can drift toward selling you more of the firm.

![Where can I hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer near me — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9313-b3.jpg)


**Executive-search and interim-leadership firms.** Traditional retained search firms increasingly run interim and fractional practices. This is the most expensive and slowest channel, but it's the right one when the role is likely to convert to full-time and you want a rigorous, references-backed process from day one.

**Warm referrals.** Your investors, board, peer CEOs, and existing revenue leaders all know fractional operators. This is the highest-trust channel because the reference is baked in and the person already understands companies like yours. The limitation is inventory — you get who your network happens to know, which may not match your motion.

**Direct sourcing on LinkedIn and communities.** Many excellent fractional CROs market themselves directly. Search "fractional CRO" plus your industry, and lean on operator communities (Pavilion is the dominant one for revenue leaders, along with RevGenius and various Slack groups). This is high-effort, high-variance, but it can surface specialists no marketplace has.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Need a fractional CRO] --> B{What matters most}
    B -->|Speed and vetted bench| C[Marketplace such as Chief Outsiders or Bolster]
    B -->|Trust and fit| D[Warm referral from investor or peer CEO]
    B -->|Systems plus leadership| E[RevOps or GTM consultancy]
    B -->|Likely to convert full time| F[Executive search interim practice]
    B -->|Niche specialist| G[LinkedIn and Pavilion community]
    C --> H[Run a paid trial engagement]
    D --> H
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I{Hit the trial goals}
    I -->|Yes| J[Sign the retainer]
    I -->|No| K[Return to channel and re source]
```

## Does "near me" even matter for a fractional CRO?

For most companies, geographic proximity is close to irrelevant, and searching by "near me" can actively narrow you away from the best operator. Fractional CROs almost universally work remotely across a portfolio of two to five clients; the operating cadence is video forecast calls, shared dashboards, and asynchronous coaching, not daily office presence. The people who insist on someone local are usually optimizing for a comfort that the role doesn't require and paying for it in a shallower talent pool.

There are three genuine exceptions where local matters. The first is field sales and outside-sales motions where the CRO needs to ride along on in-person deals, sit in showrooms, or work regional dealer and distributor relationships — proximity to your market (not necessarily your office) has real value. The second is highly relationship-driven or regulated regional businesses where in-person board and customer presence is expected. The third is simply founder preference: some CEOs coach and align far better in a room, and that's a legitimate constraint to honor even if it's not strictly necessary. Outside those cases, treat "near me" as a tiebreaker, not a filter, and spend the freed-up search radius on motion fit instead. The [remote revenue leadership playbook](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/remote-revenue-leadership) covers how to run the operating cadence when your CRO is distributed.

The more useful "near me" reframe is *near my motion*. A fractional CRO who has scaled three PLG SaaS companies from $2M to $10M is "near you" in the only sense that predicts success, even if they're three time zones away. One who is physically down the street but has only ever run enterprise field sales for a manufacturing firm is a stranger to your business regardless of the map.

## How do you vet a fractional CRO so you don't hire an expensive advisor?

The single biggest failure mode is hiring someone who talks like an operator but works like a consultant — long on frameworks, short on carrying the number. Your vetting has to force the distinction. Start by asking for their last three engagements with specifics: what the revenue was when they arrived, what it was when they left, what they personally built or fixed, and — critically — the name and contact of the CEO who can confirm it. A real fractional CRO answers in metrics and mechanisms; an advisor answers in adjectives.

Probe for motion match hard. A CRO who scaled product-led self-serve motions may be lost in enterprise field sales, and vice versa. Ask them to walk you through the specific playbook they'd run in your business in the first 90 days: the diagnostics they'd pull, the metrics they'd instrument, the first thing they'd change, and how they'd know it worked. Vagueness here is disqualifying. You also want to see how they think about your funnel math live — hand them your real numbers and watch whether they immediately spot the constraint. The [revenue diagnostics framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-diagnostics) lists the specific questions a strong operator asks in the first meeting.

Then check the guardrails that predict a good part-time engagement specifically. How many other clients do they carry, and will yours get real attention? Are they willing to be measured against concrete 90-day outcomes? Will they commit to hiring and transitioning to a full-time successor rather than making themselves permanently indispensable? Do references describe someone who was *in* the business — running the forecast call, coaching reps, sitting in deals — or someone who showed up monthly with a deck? Finally, insist on a paid trial: two to four weeks or a scoped 30-day sprint with defined deliverables, before any longer commitment. The trial is the only vetting step that can't be faked.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Candidate] --> B[Ask for last three engagements with metrics]
    B --> C[Check motion match to your model]
    C --> D[Live funnel diagnosis on your real numbers]
    D --> E[Reference calls with prior CEOs]
    E --> F{Passed all four}
    F -->|Yes| G[Run paid 30 day trial sprint]
    F -->|No| H[Pass and keep looking]
    G --> I{Hit sprint deliverables}
    I -->|Yes| J[Convert to retainer]
    I -->|No| H
```

## What does a fractional CRO cost and how are engagements structured?

Fractional CRO pricing is almost always a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days per month, and it varies widely by the operator's pedigree, your stage, and scope. The common structures are a flat monthly retainer (the most typical), a day-rate arrangement, or a smaller retainer paired with performance-linked upside. Because pricing depends so heavily on the specific operator, stage, and market, treat any single figure you hear as a data point and get real quotes from multiple candidates rather than anchoring on one number — do not let anyone, including this page, hand you a "standard rate" you didn't verify against live quotes.

What actually drives the price is the day commitment and the operator's track record. A CRO carrying one day a week for an early-stage startup is a very different line item than one carrying three days a week for a scaling PE-backed company with a full team to run. Beyond cash, some fractional CROs — especially in startups — take a small equity component, which aligns them to the outcome but should never be a substitute for them being genuinely accountable to interim targets. Watch for the misaligned incentive where an equity-heavy deal masks weak near-term accountability.

Structure the engagement to protect yourself. Insist on a defined scope of responsibilities and clear 90-day outcomes in writing, not an open-ended "advisory" retainer. Build in a trial period. Define the exit and succession explicitly — the best fractional CRO engagements have a designed endpoint where a full-time hire takes over, and a good operator will tell you that upfront rather than quietly extending their own tenure. And make sure the contract names the metrics you'll both look at monthly, so the relationship stays anchored to revenue and not to the comfort of the relationship itself. The [fractional executive engagement models](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-engagement-models) resource compares retainer, day-rate, and equity structures side by side.

One more cost worth naming: the cost of getting it wrong. A fractional CRO who is a poor motion fit doesn't just waste the retainer — they can send your team down the wrong playbook for two quarters. This is exactly why the trial-first, references-backed approach pays for itself; the fractional model's whole advantage is that a mistake is cheap and fast to unwind compared to a full-time mis-hire, but only if you structure it to be.

## Marketplace versus referral: which path should you start with?

Start with a marketplace when speed and a vetted bench matter more than a perfect warm introduction — you'll get matched candidates within days, each pre-screened for general credibility, and you can run several trials in parallel. Start with a referral when trust and motion-fit matter most and you have time to work your network, because a peer CEO's endorsement carries reference data that no marketplace vetting can replicate. Most companies should actually run both in parallel: put the ask out to your investors and peer groups the same week you open a marketplace search, then let the two channels compete on the trial.

The decision hinges on what you're most afraid of getting wrong. If your fear is speed — the number is slipping and you need an operator in the seat this month — the marketplace wins because it compresses sourcing from months to days. If your fear is fit — you've been burned by a slick hire before and you want someone whose track record a person you trust can personally vouch for — the referral wins. If your fear is systems, and you suspect the real gap is process and tooling as much as leadership, lean toward a RevOps consultancy that brings a bench plus a playbook. None of these are exclusive, and the trial engagement is the great equalizer: whichever channel surfaces the candidate, the 30-day paid sprint tells you the truth. The [GTM operating model overview](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/gtm-operating-model) can help you write the brief you hand to whichever channel you choose.

## Related questions

### How much does a fractional CRO cost per month?
It's a monthly retainer set by day-commitment, operator pedigree, and your stage — sometimes with equity or performance upside. Ranges vary widely, so collect several live quotes rather than trusting a published "standard rate."

### Fractional CRO vs full-time CRO — which do I need?
Choose fractional in the messy middle (roughly $1M-$15M ARR) where a wrong full-time hire is catastrophic. Move to full-time once revenue can justify the base plus equity and the role needs daily, undivided ownership.

### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A consultant diagnoses and leaves deliverables behind. A fractional CRO owns the number, runs your forecast call, coaches reps, and hires their own successor. Accountability for outcomes is the dividing line.

### Do fractional CROs work remotely or on-site?
Almost always remotely, across a portfolio of clients, via video forecast calls and shared dashboards. On-site only genuinely matters for field-sales, regional-relationship, or regulated motions — otherwise proximity is a tiebreaker.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Typically several months to a couple of years, with a designed endpoint. The best engagements end when a full-time successor — often hired by the fractional CRO — takes over the seat.

## FAQ

**What is a fractional CRO?**
A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is an experienced revenue executive who owns your go-to-market engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, pricing, and forecasting — on a part-time, ongoing basis, carrying accountability for the revenue number rather than just advising.

**Where is the fastest place to find one?**
Fractional-executive marketplaces like Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional, Continuum, and TechCXO. They maintain pre-vetted benches and can surface matched candidates within days, which is faster than working referrals cold.

**Does "near me" actually matter when hiring one?**
Rarely. Most fractional CROs work remotely across several clients. Proximity only matters for field sales, in-person regional relationships, regulated businesses, or genuine founder preference. Prioritize motion fit over map distance.

**How do I tell an operator from an expensive advisor?**
Ask for the last three engagements with hard before-and-after metrics and CEO references, force a live diagnosis of your real funnel numbers, and require a paid trial sprint. Operators answer in mechanisms; advisors answer in adjectives.

**Should I use a marketplace or a referral?**
Run both in parallel. Marketplaces win on speed and a vetted bench; referrals win on trust and reference-backed fit. Whichever surfaces the candidate, let a 30-day paid trial decide.

**How is a fractional CRO engagement priced?**
Usually a monthly retainer tied to committed days per month, sometimes with equity or performance upside. Pricing swings widely by operator and stage, so gather multiple live quotes instead of anchoring on any single published figure.

**When is it too early or too late for a fractional CRO?**
Too early: pre-revenue, where founders should still be selling and learning. Too late: past roughly $15-20M ARR, where the role usually needs a full-time owner. The fractional sweet spot is the scaling middle.

**What should be in the contract?**
A defined scope, written 90-day outcomes, the monthly metrics you'll both review, a trial period, and an explicit exit-and-succession plan. Avoid open-ended advisory retainers with no accountability to revenue.

**Can a fractional CRO become full-time?**
Yes, and executive-search interim practices are built around exactly that path. But the more common and often healthier outcome is the fractional CRO hiring and transitioning to a dedicated full-time successor.
